item.title: Humaiun Kobir: Bangladesh well-placed for regional connectivity
item.description:
Emphasising the growing importance of regional connectivity, Prime Minister's Foreign Affairs Adviser Humaiun Kobir on Monday said investments in transport infrastructure, aviation and digital networks are key drivers of economic growth and stronger people-to-people contacts.
"Bangladesh's strategic location provides significant opportunities to strengthen regional connectivity and expand cooperation in trade, tourism, investment and cultural exchanges," he said, noting that Bangladesh welcome greater collaboration with China and other international partners in advancing sustainable infrastructure, aviation, tourism and innovation for the benefit of the people.
Speaking as the chief guest at a joint training session's opening ceremony in the capital, the adviser stressed that future prosperity will depend not only on economic success but also on the quality of institutions, social resilience and international cooperation.
The Bangladesh Institute of International and Strategic Studies (BIISS) hosted the joint training program titled "2026 Comparative Governance Forum" at the BIISS Auditorium.
"The countries of the Global South are becoming increasingly influential in shaping global governance and sustainable development," Kobir said.
He said Bangladesh believes the international system must be more inclusive, rules-based and responsive to the aspirations of all nations. "We support multilateralism, peaceful dialogue and international cooperation as the most effective means of addressing common global challenges."
The adviser said lasting progress is achieved when nations invest in knowledge, trust and partnerships built on mutual respect.
"Economic growth creates prosperity, but wisdom, cooperation and mutual understanding are what ultimately secure peace and sustainable development," he said.
Prof Chen Zhimin, Vice-President of Fudan University, and Yao Wen, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the People's Republic of China to the People's Republic of Bangladesh, attended the opening ceremony of the joint training program as special guests.
The adviser underscored the importance of deepening Bangladesh-China cooperation through knowledge sharing, dialogue and mutual learning, saying stronger partnerships are essential to addressing increasingly complex global challenges.
He said the initiative reflects the shared commitment of both countries to strengthening academic and institutional cooperation.
"I would like to acknowledge the valuable support of the Embassy of the People's Republic of China and all our partner institutions. This forum reflects our shared belief that dialogue, knowledge and mutual learning remain indispensable in addressing the increasingly complex challenges of our time," he said.
The adviser said Bangladesh has much to learn from China's development experience while also sharing its own strengths in public policy and governance.
"Comparative governance calls for a comparative perspective on the governance systems of both countries. We can learn tremendously from the People's Republic of China. At the same time, there are areas where Bangladesh has performed well, and we should continue to build on those achievements," he said.
Describing China as one of the world's most remarkable development success stories, the adviser noted that the country has lifted around 800 million people out of extreme poverty over the past four decades through sustained reforms and economic transformation.
"China is a tremendous example of development over the last four decades. It has lifted nearly 800 million people out of extreme poverty through one of the most successful poverty alleviation programmes in history and has implemented major market reforms that have transformed its economy," he said.
At the same time, Kobir said Bangladesh has earned international recognition in several important areas, particularly disaster risk reduction and climate resilience.
"Bangladesh has become internationally recognised for reducing disaster risks and protecting lives. However, climate change is a global challenge that requires global solutions. We must continue to advocate for stronger multilateral cooperation, enhanced climate finance, technology transfer and greater support for vulnerable developing countries," he said.
Expressing optimism about the program, he said the discussions over the coming days would generate new ideas, strengthen academic and institutional cooperation and further reinforce the enduring friendship between Bangladesh and China.
Director General of BIISS Major General Ridwanur Rahman also spoke.

item.title: Some food for thought
item.description:
Walk down the lit avenues of Banani, Dhanmondi, Uttara, or Khilgaon on a Friday evening, and you will witness a city consumed by an insatiable appetite.
Neon signs flash promises of Neapolitan wood-fired pizzas, sizzling Korean barbecues, fiery Thai Tom Yum , Japanese sushi platters, and Turkish donor kebabs.
Young couples snap photographs over creamy fettuccine, while families gather around steaming pots of hotpot.
Yet, amidst this sprawling gastronomic renaissance in urban Bangladesh, a quiet, striking absence remains.
Try proposing to a group of urban Bangladeshis that tonight’s dinner out should consist of a delicate bowl of shorshe (mustard) ilish , a smoky begun (eggplant) bhorta , and a fragrant broth of river-fish curry paired with steamed miniket rice.
More often than not, you will be met with polite skepticism or outright scoffing: "Why would I pay money in a restaurant for what my mother cooks at home every day?"
This simple, reflexive dismissal reveals a deeply ingrained cultural paradox. Bangladeshis are fiercely proud of their food.
We write poetry about the fat of the river ilish; we debate the precise pungency of mustard oil; we wax nostalgic about our grandmothers’ slow-cooked winter lentils.
Yet, when we step into the public sphere as paying consumers, our native culinary heritage becomes invisible. We love our food intimately behind closed doors, but we systematically refuse to elevate it into a celebrated out-of-home dining culture.
To understand how unusual this is, one needs only to look across Asia.
Home food as public pride
In Thailand, the transition from home stove to commercial table happened with seamless elegance.
The humble street food of Bangkok -- spicy papaya salad ( som tum ), aromatic green curries, and pad thai -- did not stay confined to domestic kitchens or cheap alleyway carts.
The Thai people embraced their everyday flavours with such unpretentious pride that those same home recipes eventually gave rise to high-end bistros and Michelin-starred establishments.
A Thai diner feels no class anxiety paying premium prices for an intricately plated red curry in an upscale Bangkok lounge.
In Japan, the concept of elevating home comfort is an art form. The izakaya and the ramen-ya are built entirely around simple, rustic staples -- miso, rice, pickled vegetables, broth, and grilled fish. Japanese dining out is an extension, not a denial, of domestic sustenance.
Similarly, in Vietnam, pho and banh mi are national badges of honor, served with equal reverence on plastic stools at sidewalk corners and in air-conditioned gourmet restaurants in Ho Chi Minh City.
Even across our border in South India, the dosa and the banana-leaf meal transformed from humble home breakfasts into thriving, multi-generational restaurant chains that attract diners across all social strata.
Why, then, has Bangladesh failed to follow suit? Why have we assigned our daily native cuisine to the domestic shadows while canonizing every foreign flavor that lands on our shores?
The psychology of avoidance
The answer lies at the complex intersection of social class, colonial hangovers, and our history of domestic labour.
First , there is the devaluation of domestic labour.
For generations, traditional Bengali cooking has relied on arduous, time-consuming preparation -- grinding spices on a heavy stone shil-pata , gutting scales from river fish, and slow-simmering complex vegetable mixtures.
Because this labour was historically performed at home by uncompensated women or domestic help, urban society attached zero monetary value to it.
Subconsciously, the average Bangladeshi consumer views everyday Bengali food as something that costs nothing more than raw ingredients.
Paying a restaurant margin for lau-chingri feels like a financial scam because the domestic labour behind it has been culturally invisibilized.
Second , there is the lingering stigma of the bhat-er hotel . Outside the private home, everyday Bangladeshi food -- rice, daal , bhorta , and fish curry -- has historically existed in commercial spaces only as utilitarian sustenance for blue-collar workers, commuters, and daily wage earners.
The roadside bhat-er hotel serves a vital economic purpose, but it is unadorned and functional.
As a rising Bangladeshi middle class emerged over the last three decades, dining out became an act of social mobility and performance.
To sit in a restaurant was to signal that one had arrived. Because everyday Bengali food was associated with the working-class hustle of the bhat-er hotel , dining on it in public felt counter-aspirational.
When Bangladeshis do venture out for local food, there is one notable exception: Mughal celebratory feasts.
We readily queue for kacchi biryani , morog polao , kala bhuna , and kebabs .
But Mughal-influenced festive food is an anomaly; it represents luxury, royal indulgence, and rare celebration -- not native Bengali cuisine.
It is an escape from everyday food, rather than an elevation of it.
The first cracks in the wall
This aspirational void was eagerly filled by foreign cuisines. From the crimson-hued " deshi-Chinese " of the 1990s to modern Italian trattorias , foreign dining offered what domestic food was never permitted to offer in our minds: An escape from routine identity.
Yet, if you look closely at the modern urban canvas today, small but significant cracks are appearing in this long-standing resistance.
Consider the quiet rise of restaurants like Shodeshi and Paturi .
By packaging authentic regional Bengali delicacies -- think mustard-marinated bhetki paturi , daab chingri , and mustard-oil bhortas -- into air-conditioned, beautifully curated spaces, they are proving that urban Bangladeshis will pay for heritage when it is treated with aesthetic reverence.
Simultaneously, legacy institutions like Star Kabab remain perpetually packed across generations, proving that our craving for familiar, unpretentious comfort food never truly went away.
Even more telling is the recent phenomenon of Durbin Bangla , where crowds queue up at dawn, waiting on bench seats just to score a table for a traditional Bangladeshi breakfast.
The sight of young urbanites willingly standing in line for piping-hot rumali roti , kolija bhuna , and creamy shujir halwa over morning coffee signals a subtle cultural pivot.
Is this a true turning point, or merely a fleeting wave of social media nostalgia?
The answer likely sits somewhere in between. While these hotspots demonstrate a hunger for authentic identity, they are still the exception rather than the rule.
A few crowded breakfast halls do not yet constitute a full culinary revolution, but they do offer a crucial proof-of-concept: When native cuisine is stripped of its class stigma and presented with pride, Bangladeshis are hungry for it.
Reclaiming the table
The goal is not to abandon foreign food -- culinary curiosity is a mark of a thriving, open society.
The goal is to shed our collective lack of imagination regarding our own hearth.
We have allowed a colonial hangover and class snobbery to dictate that foreign food equals sophistication, while native food equals home boredom or working-class necessity.
Bangladesh possesses one of the most complex, seasonal, and biodiversity-rich culinary landscapes in South Asia.
The citrus-infused fish curries of Sylhet with s hatkora , the fiery chui jhal of Khulna, the herbal bamboo dishes of the Chittagong Hill Tracts, and the delicate art of winter pithas deserve to sit on fine-dining pedestals alongside any international cuisine.
Real cultural confidence begins when we step into a candlelit restaurant and feel the exact same pride paying for an exquisitely crafted shutki bhorta or a seasonal river-fish curry as we do for a plate of Italian pasta.
Until we are willing to consistently pull up a chair and dine on our own story in public, our vibrant food scene will remain a glittering hall of mirrors -- reflecting every culture in the world except our own.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune, but spends furiously on food whenever the opportunity arises.

item.title: PM appeals for public help to keep Bangladesh clean and litter-free
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday sought people's cooperation in keeping Bangladesh clean and protecting the environment, urging everyone to refrain from littering and dispose of waste responsibly to help build a cleaner and better more liveable country for future generations.
In a video message posted on his verified Facebook page, the prime minister said protecting the environment is not solely the government's responsibility but a shared duty of every citizen.
“If each of us becomes more conscious from today and disposes of our waste in designated places properly instead of throwing it indiscriminately, we can gradually make Bangladesh free of waste and build a beautiful environment,” he said.
Tarique Rahman said Bangladesh belongs to all its people and stressed that if everyone makes even a small contribution, the country would be able to achieve significant progress together.
"I seek your cooperation. Let us all work together to keep our country clean and beautiful. Let each of us do our part to protect and preserve a clean environment that will ensure a healthier, more liveable country for future generations,” Tarique Rahman said.
He said environmental cleanliness is an issue that touches people from all walks of life, as everyone is affected by the condition of their surroundings.

item.title: The July Revolution and the reinvention of national purpose
item.description:
Every generation inherits a defining historical moment. Some inherit liberation wars. Others inherit economic transformations or constitutional crises. The generation of Bangladesh that came of age in 2024 inherited something different: A civic uprising that fundamentally challenged the relationship between the citizen and the state.
Two years after the July Revolution, political debates continue over who deserves credit, who bears responsibility, and whose narrative should ultimately dominate history. Governments have changed. Political alignments have shifted. New actors have emerged while old ones have disappeared from power.
Yet if the anniversary of the July uprising teaches Bangladesh anything, it should be this: The true significance of those days extends far beyond partisan politics. The revolution ultimately became a test of whether Bangladesh could place the interests of the republic above the interests of competing political forces.
That is why "Bangladesh First" carries far greater significance than a patriotic slogan. It offers an opportunity to revisit July not simply as a political movement but as a national moment of introspection. The essential question is no longer who won or who lost. Rather, it is whether Bangladesh itself became stronger through the crisis, and whether the painful lessons of those weeks are being translated into stronger institutions, greater accountability, and a more mature democratic culture.
History repeatedly demonstrates that nations are transformed not merely by revolutions but by the lessons they choose to remember afterwards. France remembers 1789 differently from 1793. The United States remembers the Civil Rights Movement not only through legislation but through its continuing struggle with equality. South Africa continues to reinterpret the end of apartheid through debates about justice, reconciliation, and institutional reform.
Likewise, Bangladesh's July Revolution should not become frozen as a monument belonging to one political generation. It should remain an evolving national conversation about citizenship, state power, public accountability and democratic responsibility.
The greatest danger for any nation after a transformative political event is the temptation to reduce history to heroes and villains alone. Such narratives are emotionally satisfying but intellectually incomplete. They rarely explain why events unfolded as they did or why ordinary citizens suddenly became willing to assume extraordinary risks. Bangladesh deserves a more mature conversation.
The July Revolution did not emerge suddenly on August 5.
Nor was it born exclusively from the quota issue.
Rather, the quota movement became the catalyst through which years of accumulated public frustration found organized expression.
Understanding that distinction is essential for understanding modern Bangladesh.
The quota issue was never only about quotas
When the High Court restored the freedom fighter quota on June 5, 2024, many observers initially treated it as another legal controversy in Bangladesh's long history of disputes over public recruitment. Viewed in isolation, the judgment concerned administrative policy. Viewed within the broader socio-economic context, however, it touched one of the deepest anxieties facing contemporary Bangladesh.
The country's demographic reality had changed dramatically over the previous decade. Bangladesh successfully expanded access to higher education, producing hundreds of thousands of university graduates every year. Yet economic expansion did not generate public-sector employment opportunities at a comparable pace. For many young graduates, government employment represented not merely a career but economic security, social mobility, and dignity.
Consequently, recruitment policies became deeply symbolic. They represented competing visions of fairness itself.
Supporters of quotas argued that the Liberation War deserved institutional recognition and that the sacrifices of freedom fighters should continue receiving state acknowledgement. Their argument rested upon historical justice.
Opponents did not necessarily reject that history. Rather, they questioned whether historical recognition should continue shaping recruitment in ways they believed constrained meritocracy in a rapidly changing society. Their concern centred upon contemporary fairness.
Both positions possessed moral foundations.
The problem emerged because the national conversation increasingly ceased to distinguish disagreement from hostility.
Instead of facilitating constructive debate regarding balancing historical obligations with present realities, political discourse gradually became polarized between competing moral absolutes. Once that occurred, compromise became increasingly difficult.
The events that followed therefore cannot be understood merely as reactions to one judicial verdict. They reflected a deeper institutional challenge confronting Bangladesh: How should a nation honour its history without allowing historical memory itself to become a source of contemporary division?
That question remains relevant today.
From administrative dispute to national conversation
The earliest demonstrations following the June 5 verdict remained remarkably restrained.
Students organized peaceful processions, submitted memoranda, and appealed to constitutional institutions. Even during the first weeks, their strategy demonstrated an important characteristic that is often overlooked in retrospective political narratives.
The movement initially expressed confidence in the state rather than rejection of it.
This distinction deserves emphasis. Citizens protest because they expect governments to listen.
Only when they gradually lose confidence in institutional responsiveness do demonstrations begin acquiring broader political significance.
The students' memorandum to the Attorney General, their repeated appeals before the scheduled Supreme Court hearing, and their insistence upon legal remedies all suggested that the movement still believed constitutional mechanisms could resolve the dispute.
In many respects, this reflected democratic maturity rather than political confrontation.
History often forgets this early phase because later violence overshadows earlier restraint. Yet remembering it matters because it reveals that Bangladesh's institutions initially possessed opportunities for de-escalation.
Whether those opportunities were fully utilized remains a question historians will continue debating.
Why the movement spread beyond Dhaka
By the beginning of July, something fundamentally changed. The demonstrations no longer remained confined to Dhaka University.
Students from public universities across Bangladesh joined under the banner of the Anti-Discrimination Student Movement. Within days, private universities also became increasingly engaged.
Geographical expansion alone does not create a national movement. Shared emotional experience does.
The speed with which the protests spread suggested that the quota issue had become a vessel carrying broader public frustrations.
Across campuses, students increasingly interpreted the controversy as representing wider concerns regarding equality of opportunity, institutional responsiveness, youth unemployment and perceptions of exclusion.
This phenomenon deserves careful analysis.
Throughout modern history, transformative political movements rarely remain confined to their original grievances. The American Civil Rights Movement expanded beyond segregated buses. Poland's Solidarity movement grew beyond labour rights. The Arab Spring quickly moved beyond isolated acts of protest.
Not because the original issues disappeared. Rather, because they revealed deeper structural frustrations already existing beneath the surface.
Bangladesh followed a remarkably similar trajectory. The quota issue became the spark.
The combustible material already existed.
Perhaps no development illustrated this transformation more clearly than the emergence of the “Bangla blockade.”
At first glance, blocking highways appears merely as another protest tactic.
In reality, it represented an important shift in political strategy.
Modern democracies are organized around shared public spaces. Roads, railway stations, bridges and major intersections connect citizens regardless of political affiliation or social class. Once those spaces become sites of political expression, the movement inevitably enters everyday national life.
Until then, many Bangladeshis could observe events from a distance. The blockade made neutrality increasingly difficult. Office workers encountered demonstrations on their commute. Business owners experienced economic disruption. Parents worried about children travelling across cities.
Citizens previously disengaged from politics suddenly found themselves participating emotionally because politics had entered their daily routines.
Critics understandably questioned whether disrupting public life could ever be justified.
Supporters argued that extraordinary institutional inaction required extraordinary civic pressure.
Both arguments remain worthy of debate.
However, irrespective of one's political position, the blockade undeniably succeeded in transforming a student protest into a national conversation.
That strategic transformation proved historically decisive.
The crisis of institutional communication
One of the most revealing aspects of the early weeks was not the demonstrations themselves but the widening gap between institutional language and public perception.
The government largely approached the situation through administrative and legal frameworks.
Officials repeatedly emphasized that the matter remained before the courts and therefore required judicial resolution.
Constitutionally, such reasoning appeared sound. Politically, however, it increasingly failed to resonate with protesters.
This disconnect reflected a broader challenge confronting modern governance.
Institutions often respond to procedural questions while citizens increasingly raise emotional ones.
Governments speak about jurisdiction. Citizens speak about justice.
Governments discuss legal timelines. Citizens measure political responsiveness.
Neither conversation is necessarily incorrect.
The problem emerges when neither side recognizes the legitimacy of the other's concerns. Bangladesh experienced precisely that communication breakdown.
Each successive day widened the psychological distance between state institutions and student expectations.
Once such gaps become sufficiently large, even well-intentioned policy responses struggle to restore confidence.
Trust, after all, is far easier to lose than to rebuild.
The politics of language
Every political movement eventually encounters a symbolic moment that transforms its emotional character.
For Bangladesh, that moment arrived on July 14. Until then, the movement had largely centred upon policy.
Following the prime minister's remarks concerning " razakars ," the national conversation changed almost overnight.
Political language matters because words do more than communicate.They define identity.
The slogan that subsequently echoed across university campuses was not significant merely because it spread rapidly.
Its deeper significance lay in how protesters transformed an accusation into satire.
Throughout history, satire has often become one of the most powerful instruments of political resistance because it deprives authority of its monopoly over language.
The July slogan demonstrated precisely that phenomenon.
Whether one approved of the slogan or not, its impact upon public consciousness became undeniable.
The movement was no longer debating administrative policy. It had entered the far more emotionally charged territory of dignity, recognition, and national identity.
Once political conflicts become struggles over dignity rather than policy, compromise becomes significantly more difficult.
Bangladesh was approaching that threshold.
The first 40 days of the July Revolution therefore reveal a truth that should remain central to any honest historical assessment.
Contrary to many later political interpretations, the movement did not begin as a campaign to overthrow a government.
It began as an appeal for institutional responsiveness within the constitutional framework.
Only gradually, through successive failures of communication, growing polarization, expanding public participation, and escalating confrontation, did it evolve into something much larger.
Understanding that evolution matters because it contains perhaps the most important lesson for contemporary Bangladesh.
Nations are rarely destabilized by one controversial decision alone.
They are destabilized when institutions fail to recognize how individual decisions accumulate into broader crises of public confidence.
For every future government -- regardless of ideology -- that may be the most enduring lesson of June and early July 2024.
The republic is always strongest when citizens believe they can be heard before they feel compelled to be remembered.
HM Nazmul Alam is an Academic, Journalist, and Political Analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.

item.title: Oil prices fall nearly 5% after US announces new Iran talks
item.description:
Oil prices tumbled on Monday in early Asia trade after US President Donald Trump announced fresh talks with Iran to end the Middle East war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
The war, which began in late February when the United States and Israel attacked Iran, has caused oil prices to swing sharply as it effectively closed the waterway, a vital route for global oil and gas supplies.
At around 2250 GMT on Sunday, the price of a barrel of Brent North Sea, the benchmark international oil contract, for September delivery was down 4.69% at $83.81.
Its American equivalent, West Texas Intermediate, fell 4.67% to $80.72.
Trump said on Sunday that fresh negotiations with Iran will begin on Monday after holding off on major strikes against the Islamic republic to pursue a deal.
"Now what we're doing is we're talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon," he said, without providing further details of the venue of the talks or the participants.
Hours after the US had called off major strikes Iran on Sunday said it was nearing a deal with Oman over a new route through the Strait of Hormuz.

item.title: Study: 9 in 10 families borrow for measles treatment
item.description:
Nearly nine in 10 families affected by measles in Bangladesh have had to borrow money to cover treatment costs, while six in 10 depleted their savings, according to a joint assessment by the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS) and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC).
The assessment found that 89% of affected families borrowed money to pay for treatment, while 61% used up their savings.
Every family surveyed said they required financial assistance. Among them, 35% identified medicines as their top priority, followed by water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) support (33%) and food assistance (22%). Around 4% reported selling assets, while 3% relied on donations.
The assessment covered 2,746 measles-affected households receiving treatment at 12 government medical college and district hospitals across Bangladesh.
It found that the outbreak's financial impact extended well beyond medical expenses. Around 75% of patients were aged four years or below, 19% were between five and 17 years, and 6% were aged 18 or above.
The assessment was conducted to identify 2,400 of the most vulnerable households for emergency cash assistance of Tk10,000 each and to evaluate the socio-economic impact of the outbreak. Of the 2,746 households assessed, 2,400 were selected to receive assistance based on agreed vulnerability criteria.
According to the findings, affected families spent an average of Tk16,000 on treatment and related expenses. Many caregivers also reported losing income or even their jobs after spending extended periods in hospitals caring for sick family members.
Hazera Khatun travelled from Rangpur to Dhaka with her 11-month-old daughter, who is receiving treatment at Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital. The family has already spent more than Tk70,000.
"Treatment at the government hospital is free, but many other costs are not covered," she said.
"We spent nearly Tk20,000 just to reach Dhaka by ambulance. Every day we have to buy food, pay for medical tests and meet other daily expenses. I have already borrowed money from relatives. My husband works in Saudi Arabia, but he has not received his salary this month, making the situation even more difficult."
Among respondents who disclosed their occupations, 78% depended on informal employment and earned between Tk6,000 and Tk20,000 per month, making them particularly vulnerable to income loss during prolonged illness.
Dr Kabir M Ashraf Alam, secretary general of BDRCS, said the findings showed that many families were facing both a health emergency and severe financial hardship.
"Through our emergency response, we are providing cash assistance to the most vulnerable households while continuing community awareness activities," he said.
Alberto Bocanegra, head of delegation of the IFRC in Bangladesh, said the consequences of the measles outbreak extended beyond hospital treatment.
"Families often face serious financial hardship while caring for sick children or other family members. These findings highlight why humanitarian assistance and strong social protection systems are essential during public health emergencies. It is important that our response is guided by evidence," he said.
With support from the IFRC and its partners, BDRCS has assisted the government in implementing the nationwide measles vaccination campaign. The organisation has also mobilised more than 1,000 Red Crescent volunteers to conduct community awareness campaigns, support vaccination centres, and promote risk communication and early healthcare seeking.

item.title: All staff of Kashimpur land office suspended over irregularities
item.description:
All officials and employees of the Kashimpur Union Land Office have been suspended after prima facie evidence of various irregularities was found during a sudden inspection.
Deputy Commissioner Md Nurul Karim Bhuiyan on Monday said the action was taken after the inspection revealed initial evidence of misconduct in the office.
The suspended officials and employees are Acting Union Land Assistant Officer Wazed Ali Khan, Office Assistant Mostafa Kamal, Shafiqul Islam Khan and Abdul Halim.
During the morning visit, the DC inspected the Kashimpur Union Land Office and spoke to both the land office staff and people who came to receive services.
After reviewing the situation and finding preliminary evidence of various irregularities, he ordered the suspension of all four officials and employees.
Following the inspection, the DC left for another surprise inspection at the Shafipur Land Office.

item.title: Are social norms holding us back?
item.description:
In any society, laws and social norms function together to control individual behaviours, maintain societal order, and uphold the rights of the citizen.
Despite their coexistence in society, they function differently and under separate forms of authority. Law is generally a binding, formally defined set of rules backed by a controlling authority, whereas social norms are common standards of acceptable behaviour within a society that originate from shared concepts, cultural practices, or traditions.
However, when the law conflicts with social norms, people often prioritize social norms over the law, leading them to breach laws.
When it comes to law, the constitution of Bangladesh serves as the highest controlling authority to establish justice. Article 7 of the Constitution states that any law inconsistent with it is void. This article guarantees that no action can go beyond the limits of the Constitution and serves as the foundation for the country's judicial system.
However, a close examination of reality shows that while the Constitution and other laws have the authority to govern society exclusively, it does not completely control society; rather, social norms have a big influence.
In certain areas, societal norms make such a significant impact that existing laws go unenforced.
For example, child marriage remains a major issue in Bangladesh, although there exist both national and international legal frameworks to address it. To tackle this societal disorder, the Child Marriage Restriction Act was enacted in 2017. It has provisions that penalize anyone involved in child marriage.
Nonetheless, the issue persists in our society at a high rate. The current legal framework is not functioning as planned, and progress is extremely slow.
One of the main obstacles to development is our patriarchal social norms, which view marrying off girls as a solution.
The parents suffer enormous societal pressures due to many factors such as the girl's physical safety and security, financial hardships, and a lack of education. These lead the parents to arrange early marriage without considering the negative consequences of it.
As a result, societal norms take dominance over existing laws and policies intended for preventing child marriage.
Another example is the practice of dowry, which continues to pose significant challenges. The legislation enacted the Dowry Prohibition Act in 2018 but the practice of dowry persists. Several factors contribute, including patriarchal norms, family honour, societal pressures, illiteracy, etc. In many circumstances, the victim gets no legal help at all and instead face serious psychological and physical abuse, which somtimes leads to femicide or suicide.
The situation of domestic abuse is also very severe in Bangladesh, affecting many women daily. Although the legislation enacted the Domestic Violence (Prevention and Protection) Act, 2010, to specifically counter this issue, the situation nonetheless remains alarming.
Gender inequality is one of the factors that perpetuates the belief that women are inferior to men, resulting in violence against them. Domestic violence against women is often tolerated by the community, which makes it difficult to fully implement the rule of law.
Even in matters of inheritance, women in Bangladesh often find themselves at a disadvantage. Although the Constitution and other domestic laws enshrined the principles of equality and non-discrimination and took the stance of zero tolerance, the struggle of women's rights to inheritance continues. The discriminatory social and cultural norms make it challenging for women to get their legal right of inheritance.
People in Bangladesh adhere to harmful social norms like dowry, domestic violence, or child marriage simply because of the customs or practices exercised by the society. For some people, societal standards are significantly more essential than codified laws. The inclination to prioritize social norms above laws results in a weakened relationship with the law, rendering it ineffective.
Bangladesh’s legislation has consistently taken a firm stance in favour of the rule of law and intervened many times, declaring certain harmful social norms illegal. Nevertheless, the negative influence of social norms continues to overpower existing laws and policies. That negative influence poses a major challenge for the legislation to persuade those people to comply with the laws.
To make the rule of law more effective, a reformative approach needs to be taken. Enacting punitive laws and punishing the offender will not develop the situation. Rather, the people whose actions contradict the rule of law need to be reformed in a way that would gradually change the mindset and culture.
The ultimate objective should be to educate society by making the citizens aware so that they understand how some social norms negatively impact their lives. However, shifting social perceptions would not be sufficient to solve the issue; rather, the state must play a significant role.
This begins by restoring public trust in government and judicial institutions. People will only willfully challenge those negative social norms if they have trust in the judicial institutions. To achieve this, the judicial institution must become more effective and transparent.
Juwel Kobir is an advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh.

item.title: Pregnant woman dies after alleged assault by husband in Dhamrai
item.description:
A three-month pregnant woman died after allegedly being beaten by her husband in Dhamrai, Dhaka. Police have arrested the accused, Liton Sarkar.
The incident occurred in the Gomgram area of Jadabpur Union on Sunday.
Police recovered the body at night and sent it to the morgue of Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital in Dhaka for an autopsy.
According to police and local sources, Liton Sarkar works as a CNG auto-rickshaw driver.
Family members alleged that he had long been addicted to drugs and regularly subjected his wife, Popi Rani Sarkar, 27, to physical and mental abuse.
They alleged that Liton beat Popi with a stick during a family dispute on Sunday afternoon in front of their seven-year-old child, leaving her critically injured and unconscious.
Later in the evening, he, with the help of locals, took her to Kalampur Holy General Hospital, where the on-duty doctor declared her dead.
After learning of her death, locals detained Liton and handed him over to police.
The victim's father, Parimal Sarkar, alleged that his daughter had been repeatedly assaulted since her marriage.
He said she had taken shelter at her parental home several times following abuse, but returned to her husband's house after he apologised. He alleged that the latest assault led to her death.
Dhamrai Police Inspector (Investigation) Shahidul Islam said police recovered the body after being informed of the incident.
"Preliminary examination found multiple injury marks on the body. The accused husband has been arrested. The exact cause of death will be confirmed after the autopsy report is received," he said.
He added that police are in the process of recording a complaint from the victim's family and taking legal action.

item.title: For better public service delivery
item.description:
The High Court’s order for the disposal of all pending applications for new passports and passport renewals filed by Bangladeshi expatriates within 60 days is certainly a welcome intervention but also exposes a much larger, persistent problem.
Whether it is passports, land records, utility services, welfare benefits, or any other basic documentation, our public service delivery, despite lofty exclamations of digitization and reform, remains slow, fragmented, and deeply frustrating for ordinary citizens.
The expat passport backlog is only one symptom of a system that struggles to keep pace with the country’s growing population, rising mobility, and expanding digital expectations. When expatriates, who contribute billions in remittances, face delays of weeks or months for something as fundamental as a passport, we must call it what it is: A structural failure.
The same inefficiencies affect millions at home: Long queues, opaque procedures, inconsistent timelines, and a lack of accountability.
The High Court’s directive is therefore less a procedural order and more a reminder that public service delivery must be fast, predictable, and citizen‑centred.
We are a nation that aspires to reach middle‑income efficiency but that is impossible with our present outdated administrative practices.
The solution requires systemic reform, and it begins with those in charge actually caring about doing their jobs properly. Better coordination rather than operating in silos and digital systems that are fully integrated, not partially adopted, should be the minimum expectation. Citizens deserve to receive timely responses instead of bureaucratic runarounds.
Public services are not favours but rights. A modern Bangladesh demands modern service delivery, one that is transparent, efficient, and accountable, serving the best interest of the people.

item.title: Madrasa student electrocuted in Narail
item.description:
A madrasa student died after being electrocuted while attempting to repair an electric kettle at his father's tea stall in Kalia upazila of Narail on Monday morning.
The deceased was identified as Mohammad Tanvir, 15, son of Md Azgar Sheikh of Benda village in the upazila.
The incident occurred around 8am at a tea stall in Benda village under Kalia municipality.
Locals said Tanvir, an eighth-grade student, had gone to help his father at the tea stall and was preparing tea using an electric kettle. When the kettle developed a fault, he attempted to repair it and was electrocuted.
Locals rescued him and rushed him to Kalia Upazila Health Complex, where the on-duty doctor declared him dead.
Md Idris Ali, Officer-in-Charge (OC) of Kalia Police Station, said necessary legal procedures were underway.

item.title: Rafsan’s ApexStride named world champion in US-based Fowler Global Social Innovation Challenge
item.description:
Bangladeshi founder, academic, and healthcare innovator Ahmed Sajidan Jarjis Rafsan has received major international recognition after ApexStride Systems was named World Champion and Global Grand Prize winner at the Fowler Global Social Innovation Challenge in the United States.
ApexStride, founded by Rafsan, is being developed as a global MedTech innovation, health systems consulting, and implementation research platform emerging from Bangladesh for the wider Global South.
Its work connects Bangladesh, Caribbean Island communities, and South American research and policy contexts through climate-adaptive healthcare, resilient medical infrastructure, rehabilitation technology, digital health, and community-centered systems design.
According to the organizations, Rafsan’s combined work through ApexStride Systems and the Shirin Sajmila International Foundation has impacted nearly 1 million people across more than 20 countries through disaster response, rehabilitation, refugee support, women’s dignity, maternal and neonatal health, prosthetic care, education, climate resilience, and emergency medical operations.
ApexStride began with a deceptively simple question: can healthcare technology survive the real conditions of a patient’s life?
In flood-prone, high-humidity, low-resource regions, medical devices fail not only because of design limitations, but because roads collapse, follow-up systems disappear, electricity is unstable, water damages equipment, infection spreads, and patients are forced to carry the burden of broken systems.
Rafsan’s answer is ApexStride: a platform designing climate-adaptive prosthetics, medical devices, digital health systems, biomedical lifecycle infrastructure, rehabilitation pathways, technician training, patient tracking systems, and implementation research models for the places most excluded from conventional medical innovation.
The Fowler Global Social Innovation Challenge, hosted by the University of San Diego, brings together social innovators from around the world.
ApexStride emerged as global champion among teams representing more than 25 countries, receiving $25,000 in prize funding for its model of climate-adaptive mobility and healthcare innovation.
Rafsan said the recognition marks a larger shift in how Bangladesh can be understood within global innovation.
“Bangladesh is too often described only as a country vulnerable to climate disaster. I want to show that Bangladesh can also become a source of the global healthcare systems, biomedical technologies, and humanitarian infrastructure that the climate-affected world will need,” he said.
ApexStride’s first major technical focus was climate-adaptive prosthetics through their state-of-the-art biomedical innovation lab.
Its mobility systems have been designed for patients whose daily realities include humidity, water exposure, mud, sweat-related skin injury, road trauma, workplace injury, diabetes-related amputation, uneven terrain, and weak follow-up care.
The platform has expanded beyond prosthetics into medical-device lifecycle systems, digital registries, hospital-readiness consulting, rehabilitation engineering, diagnostic infrastructure, and resilient health systems design across the Global South.
Rafsan also leads the Shirin Sajmila International Foundation, a US-registered 501(c)(3) humanitarian and health systems organization named in memory of his late mother and sister. SSIF’s work spans South Asia, Africa, the Middle East and the Caribbean, and other vulnerable contexts, with programs in flood medicine, trauma care, maternal and neonatal support, menstrual dignity, refugee rehabilitation, disability education, prosthetic support, emergency logistics, and climate resilience.
The organization has supported prosthetic users, trauma survivors, refugee families, children with cancer, displaced women, adolescent girls, Indigenous artisans, climate-affected mothers, disaster-affected communities, and young people facing psychological crisis.
Its programs include post-flood medical camps, maternal and neonatal health support, menstrual dignity systems, prosthetic rehabilitation, emergency logistics, refugee trauma support, Indigenous economic resilience through Project Aranaya Kala, adolescent mental-health interventions, disability education, and field-based humanitarian operations across South Asia, Africa, and the Middle East.
During major flood responses in Bangladesh, SSIF supported 50,000 stranded families with rescue coordination, food, clean water, emergency medicines, mobile medical teams, and post-flood health camps.
Its medical operations addressed waterborne disease, malnutrition, maternal health, glucose monitoring, hemoglobin screening, neonatal oxygen saturation checks, emergency referrals, and field triage.
In Egypt, SSIF supported refugee rehabilitation efforts for Sudanese and Syrian communities, including medical and financial assistance for refugee children with cancer.
In Nepal, the organization helped mobilize a large trauma-counseling network involving psychologists and psychiatrists.
Through Project Aranaya Kala, SSIF has worked with Indigenous communities to connect cultural preservation, women’s livelihoods, natural dye systems, digital market access, and decentralized economic resilience.
Rafsan said ApexStride grew directly from the failures he witnessed in humanitarian fieldwork.
“In many communities, healthcare fails not because one device is missing, but because the entire chain around the patient collapses. Roads fail, hospitals become unreachable, follow-up disappears, devices break, infection spreads, and families are left alone. ApexStride is being built to address that whole system,” he said.
Beyond ApexStride and SSIF, Rafsan is involved in clinical and computational research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Harvard Medical School, where his work focuses on translational oncology, molecular data systems, diagnostic precision, and precision health infrastructure for resource-constrained settings.
He also co-leads Caribbean Studies Lab, an interdisciplinary humanities research platform working across Caribbean and diaspora studies, island vulnerability, climate precarity, migration governance, public health, digital inequity, and community resilience. His academic work has been presented at the prestigious international conferences including the Caribbean Digital XII Conference organized by Yale University and the ALARI IV Continental Conference at Harvard University.
This wider intellectual architecture gives ApexStride an unusual profile. It is not only a MedTech venture and not only a humanitarian platform. It is an attempt to build a new operating system for Global South healthcare, one that connects field evidence, biomedical design, public policy, climate resilience, academic research, and institutional implementation.
Rafsan’s work has also been recognized through the Ole Cup entrepreneurship competition, the Zayed Sustainability Prize shortlist in the health category, winning the Projects for Peace award, first Bangladeshi to be a Bevisioners Fellow by Mercedes Benz and other international platforms.
The significance of ApexStride lies in its refusal to treat the Global South as a passive recipient of imported innovation.
Instead, the platform begins with the real physics of vulnerable lives: floodwater, heat, humidity, fragile roads, disability, interrupted care, under-maintained medical devices, and patients who cannot afford a single system failure.
Rafsan said his long-term vision is to position Bangladesh as a producer of world-class health systems knowledge.
“Climate adaptation is not only about shelters, embankments, or emergency relief. It is also about whether a mother can reach care, whether an amputee can walk after a flood, whether a newborn can receive oxygen, whether a patient can be followed after diagnosis, and whether health systems can survive the real conditions of people’s lives,” he said.
With ApexStride’s world-champion recognition, SSIF’s expanding multi-continental humanitarian footprint, and a growing research network across medicine, public policy, climate resilience, the Caribbean, and the wider Global South, Rafsan is building one of the world's most ambitious health innovation platforms.
“This is not only about helping people after a crisis,” Rafsan said. “It is about redesigning the systems that decide who survives the next one.”
